Shot by Colored Farm Hand.
Baltimore, Md., March 31. — John Imler, a prominent farmer of Caroline county, is at the city hospital here with a bullet buried in his abdomen. Physicians say that the wound is not necessarrily fatal, but Imler is in a critical condition. John Stewart, a colored farm hand, is in the city jail, charged with attempting to murder his employer. The shooting affray occurred Sunday, and Stewart was brought here to prevent a probable lynching by Imler's neighbors.

Denton, Md., March 28.—John H. Imler, a well-known young farmer, who resided several miles north of here, was shot in the stomach this morning about 7 o'clock by Adam Stewart, a negro, whom he had employed on the farm. Stewart had manifested an ugly disposition for several days and when Mr. Imler called him to go to the field this morning he drew a pistol and fired, then fled. Mr. Imler was taken to a Baltimore hospital, but it is feared he will die. A posse of about fifty men went in pursuit of Stewart. Deputy Samuel Griffin found him in a pine thicket just north of Denton this afternoon and brought him to jail.

MR. JOHN IMLER DEAD
Mr. John Imler, who was shot on March 28th last, at his home near Ridgley, Caroline County, Md., by Adam Stewart, a young negro farm hand, died Friday morning at 6 o'clock at the City Hospital, Baltimore. Stewart, in his testimony before the jury of inquest which met at the Central Police Station Friday evening, admitted shooting Mr. Imler.

Dr. N. C. Keirle, city post mortem physician, and Dr. Edward T. West, of the City Hospital, testified that Mr. Imler died from shock and hemorrhage caused by a pistol wound in the stomach. Dr. Z. P. Henry, of the hospital, produced a signed statement of Imler to the effect that Stewart had shot him. Stewart was committed to jail to await the action of the Caroline County authorities.

WHITE CAPS AT WELLSTON.
Citizens Become Enraged and Tear Down a Negro's Tent.
The colored Baptists of Wellston recently purchased four lots in that city on which they proposed to erect a church. Albert Boyd, a negro, at once erected a tent on the lots which was to be used as a residence, preparatory to the building of the church. It is said citizens became dissatisfied with the proposed erection of the church, yet Boyd asserts that he offered to sell the lots if the building of the church was objectionable. Thursday night, while absent from Wellston, a Chandler exchange says that Boyd's tent was destroyed and his household goods piled on the ground and the following notice posted upon them:

"Notice is hereby given that those contemplating a church for the use of colored people on this property are hereby warned that the building of such a church will under no consideration be allowed by the citizens of the town of Wellston

"We hope this warning will be heeded, but if it is not and any further progress is made in the building of a church for colored people on this property sterner measures will be adopted when we next call.

(Signed) "Citizens of Wellston.

"Wellston, Okla."
albert-boyd-wellston-1903-10-09.A2:
BOUGHT FOUR LOTS.
Notice Was Posted That No Church Could Be Built.
Chandler, O. T., Oct. 15.—Some time ago the colored Baptists of Wellston bought four lots on which to build a church and Albert Boyd, a colored man put up a tent and was occupying it as a residence preparatory to building the church, says the Publicist.

Words of dissatisfaction on the part of some of the residents of Wellston had reached the ears of the colored people and Boyd says he offered to sell the lots if the church was objectionable, but as no one offered to buy he supported there was no serious objections and they were proceeding to build the church. Friday night Boyd had business out of town and during the night some party or parties destroyed his tent and threw his household furniture over the ground and then posted the following notice on the spot occupied by the tent:

"Notice is hereby given that those contemplating a church for the use of the colored people on this property are hereby warned that the building of such a church will under no consideration be allowed by the citizens of the town of Wellston.

"We hope this warning will be headed, but if it is not and any further progress is made in the building of a church for colored people on this property sterner measures will be adopted when we next call. (Signed)

"CITIZENS OF WELLSTON."

"Wellston, O. T., Oct. 8, 1903."

Boyd and other colored people from that place are here today consulting the officers in regard to the matter.

When seen Boyd said he thought he knew the parties but could not swear who did the deed. The notice was written on a typewriter and was evidently done by an amateur as the body was in full capitals while the signature was put in small letters and the punctuation was bad.

Boyd stated that he did not knew what steys his people would take in the matter as he had not consulted them further than on the subject of prosecution.

The county attorney is out of town and we could not learn what will be done.

He Severely Cut a Doctor in Dispute Over Bill.
GUERDON, Ark., April 23.—In an altercation yesterday between Dr. J. H. Guffman, a well-known physician, and Alexander Thompson, a negro, the former was seriously cut in the neck. The dispute arose over medical services, which the negro refused to pay.

alexander-thompson-guerdon-1903-04-22.A23:
NEGRO LYNCHED.
Alex Thompson Taken By a Mob and Made To Jump From a Trestle.
Gurdon, April 23.—About six o'clock this morning the body of Alex Thompson, the negro who was taken from the calaboose last night by a mob, was found hanging from the Caney Creek trestle on the Iron Mountain main line, about half a mile north of this place.

The lynching was very quietly conducted, families living in the immediate neighborhood not knowing of the affair until this morning.

Thompson was found by a negro named Haywood Dickinson, who was on his way to work at the Gurdon Lumber Company's plant at this place. Dickinson was asked if he ran after he discovered the body. He answered: "I was the first to find him, and thank God, I was the first to leave him."

As a result of the lynching the Gurdon Lumber Company had to close down today on account of having no hands. Thompson worked in the dry house at the mill.

The sheriff and coroner were telegraphed for, and arrived here at 9:30 this morning, repaired to the scene and empaneled a jury. The body was cut down, and at 11 o'clock the jury adjourned until 1 o'clock, when the examination of witnesses was begun. Most of the time was consumed in examining the guards who were on duty at the calaboose when the calaboose was surrounded by the mob. Their testimony showed that there was no possible way to tell whether whites or blacks composed the mob, as the coats of the members of it were turned wrong side out and handkerchiefs were worn over their eyes. It was very dark, and nothing was said by the party. The jury returned the following verdict: "Party came to his death at the hands of unknown parties."

Everything seems very quiet this evening, but as a precautionary measure there will be guards over the town tonight, and the sheriff will remain over until tomorrow.

Thompson was a very bad negro, and was even feared by the members of his own race. His brother arrived here today and is looked upon with suspicion. Bad blood has been brewing here for some time, as there are a great many bullies among the negroes here.

Dr. Cuffman, who was cut last night by Thompson, is getting along very well. It is thought he will be able to be out attending to his practice in a short time.

FOUGHT IN EXCURSION CROWD.
Negro Struck Man on the Head With Iron Shaker.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL. Bloomington, Ill.
Bloomington, Ill., April 12. Eugene Debs, in an interview, calls on the United Mine Workers to discipline their Linton men for the part taken in the Elks demonstration of mob violence. "The organization can do no less," he says. WILMINGTON, N. C., April 20.—Twelve convicts, three whites and nine colored, made a desperate dash for liberty early this morning, just as they were leaving the stockade at Castle Haynes, six miles from this city. One negro was killed and a white man and negro wounded. Both of the wounded escaped. Four were captured by a large posse that has been scouring the country all day, and at a late hour to-night the officers believe they have the remaining seven surrounded in a thick swamp near the northeast branch of the Cape Fear River.

The escape was planned yesterday by H. C. Martin, white, who last week was sentenced to four years on the roads for assaulting a widow woman at Delgado Mills, in this city. While the guards were taking the gang of half a hundred convicts to work this morning, the twelve prisoners in the plot made a wild dash in all directions. The remaining convicts were ordered to drop on their knees, and kept under cover by one guard, while the other guards opened fire on the fleeing fugitives, who made for the woods. John Taylor, a negro, was shot dead in his tracks, J. P. Hughes, white, and Forney George, colored, of Newbern, were shot in the back, but escaped. Taylor was serving a twelve months' term from this county for stealing chickens. Of the twelve who made the break four were from Newbern, five from Columbus and two from New Hanover.

The county commissioners have offered $50 reward for each of the white men, Martin and Hughes, and $20 each for the negroes. The sheriff's posse is very strong, and there is little chance for the convicts to escape. Pickels have been placed on all roads, and every effort is being made to capture the fugitives.

Negroes When Ordered to Disperse Reply With Voiley of Shots.
Reply With Voiley of Shots.

Muskogee, I. T., March 12.—Two deputy marshals returned to this city this morning with Frank Brown, a negro, who, it is alleged, killed Chas. Scott and wounded his father, Ben Scott, in a fight west of Checotah yesterday. The Scotts are white. Only the presence of deputy marshals prevented a lynching and a riot in Checotah last night. The shooting was done by a colored bootblack from Boise. The trouble arose over the striking of a lad from Boise by a Nampa player. A telephone message from Nampa at 12:15 o'clock this (Monday) morning states that a crowd of fifteen men made at attempt to lynch the two colored prisoners, one of whom was involved in the shooting of Officer John N. Grogan.

The fight started over an attempt by a Boise player to apologize to a Nampa player for spiking him. This led to hot words, Joe Tiner, a Boise spectator, struck Ed Ferrell of the Nampa team. Later Tiner struck Ferrell again, and a fight followed. Officer Grogan appeared with a drawn gun and kept the crowd back. Finally a Boise lad, Fritz Beal, got into trouble, whereupon a man named Luttrell of Nampa hit the boy. Quarles protested against the man striking a boy and was knocked down by several men and badly beaten.

Shooting Commences.

Grogan then fired his revolver. Some say he fired in the air, others say he aimed at Quarles, but some one struck his hand up. Quarles, while under the feet of his assailants, drew a gun and fired twice, one of the shots grazing Grogan's leg, the other going through the shoulder.

Quarles is a veteran of San Juan hill and has a good record and reputation.

Mob Storms Jail.

At 12:15 o'clock Monday morning a crowd of 15 men made an attempt to lynch two negroes, one of whom was involved in the shooting of Officer John N. Grogan. The mob secured the jailer's keys and entered the jail. When they found they could not get into the steel cell they immediately went after Chief of Police Lillard and forcibly took from him the keys to the cells.

Chief Lillard quickly gathered a number of special officers and descended upon the mob. After a lively scrimmage the crowd was driven out of the jail, and at this hour the officers appear to have the situation well in hand.

It now is feared that Grogan's wound will prove fatal. He appears to be bleeding internally.

henry-williams-nampa-1903-05-25.A12:
John R. Grogan Shot.
Nampa, May 24.—In a fight that followed a dispute over the baseball game here today between the Boise and Nampa teams Police Officer John R. Grogan was shot and severely wounded by James Quarles, colored, of Boise. The shot took effect in Grogan's shoulder, making an ugly wound.

Quarles is confined in the jail here with Harry Williams, colored, also of Boise, who was mixed up in the trouble.

After the baseball game Ed Ferrell, a Nampa player, and a Boiseite, who is said to be Joe Tyner, engaged in a fight, which attracted quite a crowd of the excursionists from Boise and Nampa people.

Grogan made an attempt to prevent what threatened to be a riot. In doing so he pushed some of the spectators back, including Quarles.

Quarles struck the officer over the head with a cane, dazing him. Grogan pulled his revolver and shot in the air, thinking by that means to put a stop to the fighting. Quarles then whipped out a gun and fired twice.

One shot grazed Grogan's knee and the other brought the officer down inflicting the wound in the shoulder.

Quarles ran but was quickly overhauled. Williams took Quarels' part in the fracas and was arrested with him.

Excitement ran high for a time and threats of lynching were indulged in, but in a short time the crowd quieted down and it became evident that no violence would be attempted.

henry-williams-nampa-1903-05-25.A22:
NAMPAS TRAGEDY
Officer Shot by a Boise Negro---The Community Controls Itself Well Under the Terrible Strain.
Last Sunday Nampa was the scene of a most deplorable and unfortunate affair, which will terminate, possibly, in the death of one good man from a bullet wound, and the execution of another man on the scaffold.

From the conflicting reports which are in circulation, it is difficult to determine the exact truth, but it seems to us that the following account is a fair version of the terrible incident:

The Boise baseball team came to Nampa last Sunday to play against the Nampa team. As is customary, a good many Boise people came down to see the game, and, as we hope is not customary, brought along a pretty large contingent of toughs. Not being able to derive sufficient excitement out of the ball game, the toughs determined on fomenting a row. In order to accomplish this end they took advantage of a quarrel which had occurred on the grounds between two of the ball players—Tyner of Boise and Ed Farrel of Nampa—but which was promptly quieted. After the game Tyner was urged to renew the quarrel and bets were placed on him that he could lick Farrel, &c. Farrel was disinclined to fight, it seems, and started away from the grounds for the apparent purpose of avoiding trouble. Tyner, however, was egged on, and went in pursuit. He overtook Farrel some 300 yards from the grandstand and with an epithet of reproach struck him a stinging blow. Farrel turned and knocked Tyner down and fell upon his prostrate form. Then the fight was on. Everybody knows what a fight in a miscellaneous crowd means. There was yelling and screaming and cursing with a general stampede to the center of attraction. Two Boise negroes—James Quarles and Harry Williams—were particularly prominent and active and wanted, it seems, to superintend the whole business. They pushed into the thick of the fray and indicated an intense desire to take a hand somewhere. One of the negroes, Quarles, managed to get into trouble with a telephone man. A Nampa contractor entered as a peacemaker and pulled the negro away. Quarles got ugly and pulled his gun. The contractor grabbed the negro's wrist and gave it such a wrenching as to make the fellow scream and promise to put up his gun and go away peacefully. The contractor let him go, but the moment he did so, the negro whipped about and shot at officer Grogan who was engaged in trying to quell the row behind. Grogan was struck in the shoulder. Several shots passed during the melee. Then some one shouted run, and the negro took to his heels. Meantime Officer Grogan was conveyed to his home where it was soon discovered that he was dangerously if not fatally hurt. He is a highly respectable man with a wife and five children, and it is terrible to think that his life has probably been sacrificed in such a way. Quarles, the fleeing negro, was soon apprehended and lodged in the city jail. Later, when the enormity of the situation became realized by the people of Nampa, their indignation was almost uncontrollable. It seemed to them that a gang of toughs had come among them for the purpose of carousing and rowing, and that a result of it was the death of a respected citizen. Nampa was aroused and that thing which always happens under such circumstances, then happened. Somebody said: "Lynch." It took—it always takes. Deplore it as we will, when the terrible mood dominates a community, there is a spell in that one word, "Lynch," which turns quiet and lawful assemblies of American citizens into nowling mobs. It wrought on Nampa. The crowd started toward the jail to mete out that awful lawless justice. But with every step, the true Americanism of Nampa gained strength and the spirit of the mob oozed out. It was but an impulse of frenzy. Before the jail
henry-williams-nampa-1903-05-25.A23:
was reached it had almost died away. It clung to a few who made a half-hearted little demonstration on the jail—just as an earnest of good faith—when the crowd vanished into the night, ashamed of its own shadow, and the Nampa mob was but a memory of the past.

Probably no community, under such a terrible strain, ever behaved better than did Nampa on that occasion. There never was a more magnificent demonstration of inbred respect for law and order. Nothing could be more creditable to our western civilization.

Quarrels, the negro, is now in the county jail awaiting preliminary examination.

An amusing and contemptible effort has been made on the part of the Boise newspapers to show that a spirit of lawlessness rages in Nampa; and every day those papers break out in a cold sweat fearing that Nampa is going to rise up in the night and do deeds of bloody violence. A recent issue of the Boise press heard such deep and ominous rumblings as struck terror to the heart of Jim Hawley who in the midst of a grandiloquent peroration, prepared by Puckett, turned ghastly red and asked the court to adjourn while he went down to Caldwell to ask his client how it looked to him, or words to that effect. The court adjourned, and immediately Attorney General Bagley had a few spasams and broke wildly for the telephone, shouting "Watkins, Watkins, the Department of Justice of the State of Idaho is looking for Watkins, the sheriff of Canyon County." And Watkins said, "What the devil is the matter with you." The Boise press says gravely that Quarrels must be taken to Boise. We think so too. If his being here in Caldwell is going to keep the capital of the state in white livered connipitions, for heaven's sake let him go to them to quiet their wild alarms.

It is proper to say in seriousness that the attitude of Boise newspapers in this matter is disgusting. Canyon county is quite able to take care of her own affairs. The people of Nampa are of the people of Canyon, and among us we will maintain the majesty of the law. There is no mob spirit anywhere in this county. If Boise would do us a favor, let her keep her hoodlums at home. We'll attend to ours.

NEGRO FINED $150.
Boise, Idaho, Dec. 11.—At Caldwell today Judge Stewart sentenced James Quarles, the Boise negro, to pay a fine of $150. The amount was paid. Quarles was convicted of assault with a deadly weapon with intent to commit bodily harm for shooting officer Grogan in Nampa last May. isaac-adkins-fishkill-1903-12-10.A1:
JUDGE SAVES NECRO FROM MOB Adjourns Examination and Orders Officers to Hurry Man Accused of Attacking White Girl to the Poughkeepsie Jail.
Only quick action on the part of Justice Norris prevented the lynching of a negro at Fishkill by the citizens of that place. A rope had been purchased, the hangman's knot tied in it and the place of execution had been selected.

Isaac Adkins, a negro, thirty-five years old, was the intended victim. He is now held in the Dutchess County Jail at Poughkeepsie charged with attacking Miss Cora Wallace, seventeen years old, of Fishkill.

Miss Wallace is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Wallace. She met Adkins on the street in Fishkill and asked him to tell her where her father was working.

Adkins told her Mr. Wallace was working in an old cemetery, and offered to show her where he could be found. When they reached a secluded spot in the old burying ground he attacked her. Her screams frightened him off and brought a number of men hurrying to the spot.

After hearing Miss Wallace's story the men organized an armed posse and started in pursuit of Adkins. He was found hiding in the woods near Brinckerhoff, nearly ten miles from the scene of his attack on Miss Wallace. He was taken back to Fishkill and arraigned before Justice Norris.

In the mean time the report of the negro's attack on Miss Wallace had spread through Fishkill, and an angry crowd gathered outside the Justice's office. One of the most prominent citizens of Fishkill furnished the money with which to purchase a rope and another tied the hangman's knot in it. A spot was selected on which to hang the negro, and the crowd then started back for the Justice's office.

Justice Norris had heard the angry murmuring of the crowd, and without waiting to finish the examination had held the negro for the Grand Jury and advised the officers to slip out the back way with their prisoner and hurry him to Poughkeepsie. This was done, and the crowd was kept waiting until the prisoner was well on his way.

On the train the negro constantly begged the officers with him to save him from the mob.

Henry Wallace, father of the girl, is almost distracted over the attack on his daughter. Usually a quiet and reserved man, he was with difficulty prevented by friends from going to Poughkeepsie to kill the negro.

"I fought four years in the civil war to free the negroes, and this is my reward," he said as he paced up and down the front room of his home.

It is feared another attempt will be made to lynch the prisoner, several citizens having volunteered to lead a mob to Poughkeepsie for the purpose. Miss Wallace is suffering from nervous collapse.

THE Jersey City News. SATURDAY. DECEMBER 12. 1903. Union League Atraoity.
The action of the Union League Club of New York in deliberately forcing a new sectional warfare over the Negro issue, is abominably wicked. It would be criminal if it were sincere. As it is miserably hypocritical, it is not only criminal, but outrageous.

The attitude of the North is not one bit different from that of the South towards the Negro. We have no more love and far less sympathy, or toleration, for him. We are just as ready to lynch him—as was shown at Fishkill on Thursday. We are just as unwilling to associate with him, and if there were the least chance of his getting political control of any place, State, County, city or village, we would be just as ready as the Southerners to convince him with the shotgun that he is an inferior and must be content with his lot. Would the Union League Club admit, say Booker T. Washington, to membership?

The difference between North and South is that they are neither a danger nor a nuisance to us. Free, they are a daily, hourly, menace to the South. Out of power, they are this; in power, they would be such a brooding horror that the whites would probably rise and massacre them.

The proposition of the Union League Club appears to be that the United States Government should ignore everything that the Constitution stands for, and taking the Southern States by the throat dictate their internal policy—dictate it, too, not in a beneficent way, but for their ruin.

What is the Republican party aiming at? Does it desire to compel a new secession? Does it see in another bloody war the only hope of its own perpetuity in power. Let its leaders take warning. A war to fasten Negro supremacy upon even one Southern State would find as many men arrayed against the outrage in the North and West as in the South itself.

j-d-mayfield-danville-1903-07-25.A2:
MOB LOOSE IN DANVILLE.
ONE NEGRO LYNCHED.
Rioters After Another to Hang Him Three Badly Beaten.
Danville, Ill., July 25.—This city is in the throes of a race riot. One negro, an unknown man from Evansville, Ind., who to-night shot and killed Henry Gatterman, white, has already been lynched by a mob of six hundred men, who were later fired upon by the sheriff, three men being wounded. The mob was clamoring for the life of another negro, James Wilson, who has confessed to a brutal assault on Mrs. Thomas Burgess, wife of a farmer at Alvon, Ill., just north of here.

The unknown negro met his fate while the mob was on the way to lynch Wilson. The angry throng was passing Jown East Main-st., when the negro became involved in an altercation with some of its members. They started after him and he pulled a gun, firing into the crowd. Henry Gatterman, a butcher, who recently returned from Fortress Monroe, fell mortally wounded, and expired in a few seconds.

The negro fled, but was caught by the officers within a block of the scene of the tragedy and hurried to the police station, with the mob in hot pursuit, temporarily diverted from their march to the county jail. The officers, with their prisoner, took refuge in the City building, barricading themselves behind the door of one of the offices. They could not check the mob, however, for it secured a long pole and started to batter down a section of the wall and the door, both of which were very thin.

On account of the overwhelming number of the mob, it was useless for the officers to resist.

The negro was seized and rushed to the spot where he had shot Gatterman. It was the work of an instant to throw a rope around his neck and swing him up to the nearest telephone pole. He was left hanging, while the mob proceeded on to the county jail. The officers hope to save the second negro by some ruse.

Wilson, it is charged, went to the Burgess farmhouse while Mrs. Burgess was alone and told her that he was hungry. While she was getting him something to eat he entered the kitchen door and seized her. He fled, leaving her half dead. She managed to crawl to the nearest farmhouse, where she told the story. A posse of officers captured the negro and hurried him to the county jail, to prevent lynching. There the negro confessed.

Three other negroes have been attacked by members of the mob and severely beaten. Two are said to be refugees from Evansville, Ind. Some negroes are arming themselves and others are preparing for flight.

The Evansville victim of the mob was later identified as J. D. Mayfield. The mob changed its mind before attacking the jail and went back and cut down Mayfield's body. They rushed it to the public square and burned it in a bonfire, hacking it to pieces as it burned. Then they charged the jail, and the Sheriff and deputies fired, wounding several members of the mob, some fatally.

The mob threatened to lynch the Sheriff, his deputies and the negro turnkey.

After securing battering rams, it took the mob about half an hour to wreck the city prison, the negro being found hid in a safe. He was pulled from the safe, struck with sledges, knocked down, jumped upon and stamped to death. A rope was placed around his neck and his lifeless body was dragged three blocks through the streets to the scene of the shooting. An effort was made to hang the body to a telegraph pole, but the rope broke. The mob, which by this time numbered five thousand, then dragged the body to the jail and burned it.
j-d-mayfield-danville-1903-07-25.A3:
DEADLY VOLLEY FIRED
FIVE MEMBERS OF THE MOB SERIOUSLY WOUNDED.
Others Supposed to Have Been Carried Away—Sheriff Commended—The Jail Battered.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

DANVILLE, Ill., July 25.—A big, burly negro named Metcalf was lynched to-night and his body burned. Later an attempt was made to enter the jail and secure another negro, but the effort proved fruitless and several members of the mob were seriously wounded by the sheriff and his assistants. The mob received fair warning, but failed to heed it, and a volley was fired into the crowd that was battering at the jail.

About 8:30 p. m. Metcalf became involved in an argument with Henry Gatterman, a young German butcher, in front of an East Main-street saloon. The dispute ended in the negro shooting Gatterman dead. Metcalf was caught, and with much difficulty the police took him to the city prison, followed by a crowd, which rapidly grew into a mob that yelled itself hoarse in demanding that the murderer be lynched.

The police, assisted by Sheriff H. H. Whitlock, who were gathered in the city building, attempted to keep the mob out, but were finally forced to admit a portion of the crowd. The murderer had previously been locked in a vault in which the police records are kept, and the officers hoped the mob would not find him.

The leaders were told that Metcalf had been taken out of the rear door and carried into the country in a buggy, but they refused to believe the assertion. Some went for railroad irons and others for sledge hammers, and a few minutes later the lock had been knocked off the vault door and the negro was dragged forth, amid the exultant shouts of his captors. The victim made a fierce struggle, but the blows that were rained upon him soon brought him to the floor of the police station and a revolver in the hands of one of the members of the mob put a sudden end to his sufferings.

HANGED AND RIDDLED.

The mob then dragged the dying negro from the building and, placing a rope about his neck, dragged him one square south to Main street and thence five squares east to the saloon where he killed Gatterman, where his body was strung up to a telegraph pole and riddled with bullets.

Cries of "Burn up," "Burn up," were then heard and the mob leaders soon had the lifeless body of the negro cut down and were dragging him south on the Wabash railroad tracks. At South street the mob leaders decided to take the body to the jail where another negro, captured at Marshfield, Ind., charged with trying to outrage Mrs. Mary Burgess, a white woman, yesterday, was confined.

As soon as the word was given the mob yelled, "To the jail;" "Mob the other nigger," etc., and made a wild charge for that building, where quite a crowd had already congregated in anticipation of another lynching. Arrived at the jail the body of the negro was placed in the center of the converging streets, where dozens of frenzied men and boys kicked and jumped upon it. The body was naked and blood was oozing from dozens of bullet holes.

THE EODY BURNED.

Some one then threw an armful of hay upon the body and touched a match to it, after which the mob backed away a short distance and watched the awful spectacle.

Growing tired of this gruesome spectacle the mob turned its attention to the county jail and demands were made upon Sheriff Whitlock that he should give them the alleged rapist. A dozen or more deputies and policemen had hurriedly been placed in the jail all heavily armed.

As the clamor for the second negro grew louder and more incessant Sheriff Whitlock stepped out upon the veranda of his residence, which is in the east side of the jail, and, calling for silence, said: "You are doing wrong. You will regret what you have already done to-morrow, and you should go home and allow the law to take its course. This negro has not been identified as the man who assaulted Mrs. Burgess. If he had been I would turn him out to you. You cannot afford to kill an innocent man."

Anarchy, Mob and Lynch Law Is Increasing In Illinois
Anarchy, mob and lynch law with all of its hideousness again raised its slimy and bloody head at Danville, Ill., last Saturday night. A Negro by the name of J. D. Mayfield, late of Evansville, Ind., became involved in a quarrel with a white man by the name of Henry Gatterman, and the former

pulled out his revolver and shot the latter dead in front of the saloon in which Mayfield had been refused a drink. The officers of the law promptly arrested Mayfield and lodged him in the city prison. Unpardonable Crimes
Assault on women and the unprovoked killing of men are unpardonable crimes. They deserve the severest penalties that can be inflicted, and it is almost sure that if the law could be left to take its course the miscarriage of justice would be the exception, not the rule. Frenzied men might not under no circumstances be satisfied, but cool and candid deliberation would much more likely to reach a correct verdict than that of a mob in the heat of passion. Men still have left not only the sense of justice, but respect for their oaths. But the mobs sometimes get the upper hand of officers and conservative citizens, and deal summarily with culprits, thus defying all law and order.

Lynching has been all too common in our southern land. But if we have not misread the papers, they have been more numerous down south simply because the crimes that provoke them are more numerous down here than up north. Not long ago it was thought that a lynching up north was next to impossible. But human nature, despite Boston and the teachings of men in other places, is the same on one side of the dividing line as on the other, and lynching is the penalty meted out occasionally to culprits for other crimes than assault upon women. And more than once in the past few months innocent negroes have been driven from their homes, and otherwise suffered at the hands of their northern friends.

A few days ago a brute assaulted and outraged an innocent girl. The wrath of the citizens was aroused, and quickly as posible after his capture he was taken from the officers and hanged-in and orderly manner. Not a shot was fired, nor was he othermaltreated. The lynching simply expressed the determination of the people to avenge a horrible crime. The lynching was unjustifiable. These determined citizens could have been equally as efficient in demanding the execution of the law at the hands of judge and jury. This was in Mississippi.

But a worse thing has just transpired in Illinois. The county Superintendent of Public Instruction in Belleville declined to renew the license of a negro schoolteacher, whereupon the negro shot the superintendent. He was arrested and jailed. Two mobs gathered. The first failed in their object; the second succeeded. In the struggle that ensured the negro was hit on the head with a sledge hammer, and led out more dead than alive. He was string up to a telegraph pole. A fire was built, and before the man was dead he was cut down, saturated with coal oil, and thrown on the fire. While yet in agony, and groaning, the mob fell on him with clubs and knives, and beat and cut the burning body almost to pieces. This unpardonable crime was committed in the North. The heart sickens. Comment is unnecessary.—Christian Advocate.

Interesting Letter from the Husband of the Injured Lady.

Editor of The Times-Dispatch:

Sir,—Many conflicting statements have appeared in your paper concerning the attempted criminal assault on Mrs. C. E. Geoghegan here on the night of July 23d, and as none of them have given all the facts in the case, I wish therefore to place before the executive office of this State and the people, the facts as proved at the trial.

I went to see Doc. Bacon about 8 o'clock the next morning after the attempted assault, as I had heard there was meal on his hat and head. 'When he saw me coming, he walked quickly to a nearby stable, picked up a stick and took his position where I first saw him. I walked up and said: "Doo., why didn't you stay at my house last night?" His reply was: "I wish to God I had." He said: "Who do you think did it?" I said: "I haven't the slightest suspicion." He said (without any cause whatever, as far as I know): "Anderson Finch was in town last night."
Now, Anderson Finch had not been here for about a year, and I had not even suspicioned his presence. I asked Doc. how he knew. Doc. said that he saw him at the depot the night before; that he came to town Saturday night before; he saw him get off the 12 o'clock freight. While talking with Doc. I saw something like meal on his hat, but still did not suspect him of the crime.

A little later, Anderson Finch was arrested out about one and one-half miles from town, hid in a barn. The gentlemen who arrested him testified at the trial that Anderson said he was not surprised at being arrested, as he had heard that Doc. Bacon had been telling lies on him. Later, he admitted his guilt and implicated Doc. Bacon, as per his statement on the witness stand as follows:

He said Doc. and he got together at the depot and Doc. had something in a paper bag under his arm and asked him to go with him to Mr. Geoghegan's to see his (Doc's) wife. (Now, Doc. had sent his wife out in the country the evening before to remain until Saturday; she was to have gone Thursday afternoon; but for some reason, not known, went Wednesday evening of the night of the attempted assault.) Anderson said he asked Doc. what he was going to Mr. Geoghegan to that hour (11 o'clock) to see his wife for. Doc. said: "Never mind; you come on and go with me." They went, and Doc. stationed him in front of the house, with instruction to whistle if any one came along. (Doc. knew that I had been kept out late at night for some two weeks rehearsing for a drama to be given the next night after this.) Doc. then went into the porch and when Mrs. Geoghegan came out to resume her seat on her front porch waiting for my return, Doc. pulled the chair back and threw the meal in her eyes. At the same time he caught her by the throat. She screamed two or three times and in the scuffle, which followed, the baby was awakened and orled, and Doc. gave her a kick and said: "Go to your d—— baby." (Doc. knew that every child I had would recognize him, therefore, he was afraid to enter the house. They did not even know Anderson Finch, for they are all young and had not seen him for a long time.)

The above statement by Anderson was in corroboration of Mrs. Geoghegan's statement except she did not remember making any sound, although she tried. After Anderson admitted his guilt and implicated Doc., I remembered his ick-ing up the stick, presumably to defend himself; and his mentioning Anderson's name and Anderson naming him, was conclusive evidence of his guilt to my mind. But this was not all. Several witnesses testified that they saw meal on Doc's, hat and head. Two testified that meal was in his pocket and in his knife. Even the bran from meal was found in his knife. Others testified to seeing two men near John Reeks' stable (about four squares from my house) at 11:15 or 11:30, with a lantern, which was turned low, while they were passing. Both, Anderson and Doc, admitted that they were the two.

Doc, had three witnesses, the first to prove that he was at the depot at 9 o'clock. Witness said it was 9:30. The second swore that Doc, went to her house at 9 o'clock and did not leave until after 12, while Doc, himself testified that he met all the trains, which are 9:25, 0:55 and 11:55 P. M. The third was to prove that he threw the meal on Doc., one Budd Donaldson, and he testified that he had never thrown meal or anything else on Doc. Now, here comes what is said to be now light on the case, viz: 'That two negroes and a white boy will testify that one John Lee threw the meal. I am reliably informed that they will testify that it was flour and not meal thrown on him. This was five days before the assault, therefore, this would not account for meal on Doc.'s hat, in his head, in his pocket and in his knife. Doc. also testified that he did not go to my house that night at all, while a witness said he saw him come out about 0 o'clock. Doc. told Mrs. Geoghegan that evening that he had to drive a good part of the night and would not return home. Mr. W. B. Penick, who employed Doc., will testify that Doc. told him that same evening that he could not work, as he was going away; also told him next morning that he did not go to the stable at all that night. A lady will testify to very indecent conduct in my front yard that afternoon about 2 o'clock by Doc. Bacon.

I do not want any innocent man punished, but with the testimony, as herein stated (and if any man doubts any part of it, if he will come to Chase City, I will verify every whit, if not, I will pay his expenses), how can any man doubt for a moment Doc. Bacon's guilt? If he is innocent, who then is the murderer of Anderson Finch, who is in his grave, and against whom there was not a word of testimony except his own statement and that of Doc. Bacon?

I do not wish to criticise any official, but I think Mr. Montague made a mistake when he granted Doc. Bacon a respite without first communicating with our county judge, who sat on the case, and I think that he should express
self. I think, further, that Mr. E. C.
Goode made a greater blunder when he
asked for the respite, because of a talk
with one Mr. Rahilly and Doc. Bacon, for
where is the man that will not plead his
innocence as long as hope is held out to
him?

Yours very truly,
C. E. GEOGHEGAN.
Chase City, Va., September 7, 1903.

PETERSBURG, VA., September 15.--Charles Bacon, Doc Bacon's brother, visited him in the jail in this city today. Charles Bacon is a respectable looking negro, slightly older than his brother. Last Friday Deputy-Sheriff Robert Milsted had occasion to go and see James, at the latter's house, concerning a cow. While there he noticed that James' buggy was minus the required road tax tag, and called his attention to the fact, explaining the law to him. The nigger replied saucily that it was none of the deputy's business whether he had a tag or not. Milsted, to make sure, returned to the barn and took a second look at the vehicle, convincing himself that the tag was not there. When he returned to where the negro was, in a lane near the house, he found him cursing the Sheriff and all the court and deputies. On seeng Milsted, he at once advanced toward him, and in a jiffy had him around the waist, declaring that he would cut his throat. Milsted pulled his pistol and shot, without aiming. Hardly had the deputy landed on the ground before the negro was on top of him attempting to draw his knife, and declaring that he would cut his throat. Milsted, on getting up, saw the brother of the negro coming in that direction with a shot gun, and of course he vacated that neighborhood.

RACE WAR THREATENS THE CITY
White Men Warn a Colored Man to Leave His Home.
NO NEGROES WANTED
Officials Present but Not in Force to Act.
Oklahoma City, O. T., Aug. 1.—At about 1 o'clock Friday morning an episode occurred in Orchard park which indicates that the breaking out of race troubles in other parts of the country, may be expected at any time in this city, says the Oklahoma.

Wibur Shepard, an employee at the Delmar Garden theatre was returning to his home after the performance late Wednesday night. He saw a number of armed men out by the woolen mill on West Main street, and not being able to distinguish them clearly in the darkness, concluded they were strange tramps and was mue alarmed over the discovery, as himself and wife reside in an isolated locality in the western suburbs of the city.

His wife being with him Shepard returned to the store at the corner of Main street and Western avenue and telephoned to Deputy Sheriff at Delmar Garden.

The deputy summoned a policeman at the park and, accompanied by two other men proceeded to the locality where the armed men had been seen.

In a short while they located a party of men in the front of a small frame house and were engaged in an angry conversation with its occupant, who proved to be a negro.

From the drift of the conversation it was discovered that the midnight visitors were ordering the negroes to remove from the neighborhood and threatening rough usage in case the warning should not be heeded. They gave the negroes twenty-four hours in which to remove with their belongings from Orchard park, which, they declared, was a white man's residence district and should remain so at any cost.

The officers approached the party and endeavored to throw a flash light upon the leaders of the party, but immediately found themselves looking into the frowning muzzles of a dozen winchesters and received the order to "git," which command they lost no time in obeying, regarding it as foolhardy to attempt to arrest any of the men in the party who were all seen to be masked and thoroughly armed.

The officers differ in their estimate of the number of men in the party, the policeman declaring his belief there were twenty-five, while deputy sheriff thought there were forty. The west end resident who first saw the armed party says there were about a dozen men in all.

The matter was presented to the city and county authorities and a deputy sheriff and a policeman were detailed to visit the scene again last night. In case a party was assembled to molest the negro resident the officers were instructed to command the peace and if necessary request the marauders to submit to arrest, but were warned not to imperil their lives unnecessarily.

The officers visited the locality at about eleven o'clock last night, but there were no signs of a recurrence of the visit by the mob. It is not believed by the authorities that the incident is closed, however, as the spokesman of the mob in his warning to the negroes the night previous, said; "We may not return tomorrow night, nor the next night, nor the next night, nor the night following, but we will return again soon and if you do not pack up and get out of here you will regret it."

The officers who encountered the party of armed and masked men on Wednesday night or Thursday morning, as it occurred after midnight, say they seemed terribly in earnest and do not doubt that there is trouble ahead. The authorities, however, are disposed to prevent any violence and will undoubtedly dispatch a posse of deputies and squad of police men to the locality at the first intimation of trouble.

It is said that there are two negro families residing in the house which was visited and they did not move out yesterday nor manifest any inclination to do so.

Oklahoma City, O. T., Aug. 13.—The situation here in reference to race troubles has been slightly improved, but negroes have appealed to people and police for protection from dynamiters who have operated in Orchard park. An effort is being made to stop all trouble between whites and negroes and if necessary summary measures will be used by authorities in Oklahoma City.

The following appeal has been issued by the negroes:

To the best citizens and highest citizenship of Oklahoma City we appeal:

Gentlemen:—We know that the liberty loving and law abiding citizens in this, our fair city, are far in the majority. We know that said citizens are jealous of the good, name, the progress and brilliant future of this, now buding and promising city. We know that in every city, irrespective of locality, there are some men, white and black, who disregard the laws of the land and perpetrate deeds which the best citizenship would not indorse, would not stand by. We come to you, liberty loving law abiding, peaceable citizens and represent:

That we are law abiding citizens.

That we too are anxious about the future of this, Our Fair City.

That we have let our buckets down here, have cast anchor and ask you to entreat us not to leave you, for all we have is here.

That we are striving to build a better citizenship, a more progressive, a more industrious, a more frugal, a more respectable, a more representative that we have hitherto had, or than any other city has under Our Flag.

That we are trying to accomplish these things through your encouragement, your aid, your protection.

That by the sweat of honest toil, we have bought our homes, not palaces and mansions; but sacred and dear to us. In these we sit around our fire hearth and talk of the past. We fondle our little ones, as they prattle on our knees and hope for the future.

These homes, though commonplace, these fire hearths, these children, we call on you to protect.

A few days ago one of hese law abiding citizens, purchased of a white citizen a piece of property in Orchard park. The vendor never once intimated that the vender would not be allowed to live on said premises, but rather encouraged the purchase as a step towards that which was commendable. We submit that we cannot build costly mansions, but we are neat and clean in these we have and will enlargen our borders as opportunities present themselves.

Not that they are especially offensive, not that they are disturbers, not that they are loud and boisterous, but that they are simply negroes. Gentlemen: To our minds, according to our interpretation of Americanism, this lawlessness strikes at the foundation of our government and seeks to throttle the life out of our fair city in its infancy. This is lawlessness starting as a mere speck on the distant horizon is destined, if not checked pow, to rise and gather momentum. We call on you, we call on you now, we call on you as deserving citizens of your city to scatter that speck of a cloud brewing on youder horizon and let the sunshine in. NEGRO WOUNDED BY POSSE. Sheriff Captures Robert Bishop After Desperate Fight.
Robert Bishop, the negro who shot Samuel Ellis and a woman known as "Black Ida" in a graders' camp at Oakville, St. Louis County, last Friday night, was captured yesterday by the Sheriff of Ste. Genevieve after a desperate fight.

During the encounter Bishop was shot four times by the Sheriff and his posse, who had shotguns loaded with buckshot, according to information which reached the Sheriff's office in Clayton.

After Bishop shot Ellis and the woman he fled to avoid lynching, as the other graders tried to hang him and pursued him for a mile with that purpose. He escaped in the forests along the Mississippi River and continued southwardly.

Constable John Schaper of Carondelet Township sent the negro's description to Seward Missouri office, from which this Bishop was recognized when he appeared in the vicinity of Ste. Genevieve. The Sheriff was notified and organized a posse to capture Bishop. They found him in a clump of bushes on the outskirts of the town and called upon him to surrender.

In answer Bishop drew a 41-calliber bulldog revolver from his pocket and opened fire. The posse returned it, and in the melee four shots were buried in the negro, seriously wounding him. He was taken to a hospital.

Constable Schaper departed for Ste. Genevieve yesterday evening to bring Bishop back.

Negro Who Is Supposed to Have As-saulted Two Women.
ST. LOUIS, June 23.—Two women, one white and the other black, were assaulted and left for dead about three and a half miles east of East St. Louis this afternoon, and a posse is out hunting for a negro described by one of his victims. If he should be captured it is believed there will be a lynching, for the terrible double crime has caused great excitement and indignation among the farmers of the American bottoms, where it occurred.

One of the victims, Mrs. Annie Green, a colored woman aged twenty-five, was clubbed about the head, her skull fractured and left arm broken. Just before relapsing into unconsciousness she told of the assault and described a light yellow negro aged about twenty-five years as her assailant. She was evidently the first victim of the negro, who later proceeded to the home of John Bruno, a well-to-do farmer living between East St. Louis and Belleville, and committed the second crime.

About 3 o'clock this afternoon a brother of Miss Florence Bruno, aged seventeen, returned home and found his sister lying on her bed in an unconscious condition. Her skull was fractured, both arms were broken and she was suffering from other injuries. The young woman had been at home alone during the afternoon tending to the family washing. She was her father's housekeeper. Young Bruno spread the alarm, and then the other assault became known. A posse was rapidly summoned, and the country thereabout was searched for the guilty man.

To-night the posse of farmers, reinforced by the chief of police of East St. Louis and members of his force and the sheriff of St. Clair county, with a number of deputies, surrounded a man on an island formed by backwater from the Mississippi flood. It is not known who the man is.

Florence Bruno was taken to St. Mary's Hospital in East St. Louis. She was still unconscious at a late hour to-night, and, though the physicians have done everything possible for her, they express no hope for the girl's recovery. Annie Green, who is at the Henrietta Hospital in East St. Louis, is in a precarious condition, but there is a chance for her recovery.

If he is captured it is believed there will be lynching, for the double crime has caused great indignation among the farmers of the American bottoms, where it occurred.

One of the victims, Mrs. Annie Green, a colored woman, aged 25, was clubbed about the head, her skull fractured and left arm broken. Just before relapsing into unconsciousness she told of the assault and described a light yellow negro, aged about 25, as her assailant. She was evidently the first victim of the fiend, who later proceeded to the home of John Bruno, a well-to-do farmer, living between East St. Louis and Belleville, and committed the second crime.

About 5 this afternoon a brother of Miss Flora Bruno, aged 11, returned home and found his sister lying on her bed in an unconscious condition. Her skull was fractured, both arms were broken and she was suffering from other injuries. The young woman had been at home alone during the afternoon, tending to the family washing. She was her father's housekeeper.

The posse late tonight surrounded a man supposed to be the fleeing negro on an island formed by the backwater from the Mississippi flood.

Henry Griffin, a negro 27 years old, supposed to know something of the assault made upon Florence Bruno, a white girl, and a negress, at East St. Louis Tuesday, was arrested yesterday afternoon at the foot of Lucas avenue and is locked up at the Carr Street Police Station.

He is a yellow-skinned negro, big boned and quite tall. He is unable to give a clear account of himself at the time the assault was committed.

An officer from the East St. Louis police force was unable to identify him from the description given by Annie Green, the negress who was assaulted. He will probably be taken to East St. Louis to-day to give the Green woman a chance to identify him.

When questioned by Lieutenant Mansfield of the Fourth District last night, he told conflicting stories. He is what is termed a "typical negro tramp."

He said he came to St. Louis the night the assault was committed in company with another negro, over the 'Frisco Railroad. He admits having been in East St. Louis for four weeks, four months ago. He said while he was there he did nothing but beg.

He said he served three years in the Reform School at Pontiac, Ill. On May 25 he was released from the Workhouse at Kansas City. He is unable to give an account of himself for twelve days since that time.

The officer from East St. Louis stated that Annie Green, the negress, said that the negro who assaulted her wore a pair of corduroy trousers and a brown hat. The negro who is held has on a pair of trousers that at first sight would easily be mistaken for corduroy trousers. He wore a dilapidated black derby.

He will probably be taken to Police Headquarters this morning and "sweated," and from there he will be taken to East St. Louis.

It is thought that if he is not identified for this crime, he is guilty of some other, and will probably be held until he can give a clear account of himself. He does not know any one in St. Louis.

VICTIM IS DEAD.

Miss Florence Bruno, the 17-year-old daughter of John Bruno, who was assaulted by the negro in her home near the Four-Mile Crossing, East St. Louis, died at St. Mary's Hospital yesterday morning.

The girl's skull had been fractured and a knife blade had been thrust to its hilt in each temple. She was unconscious when found and remained so until she died.

Hundreds of farmers and citizens, led by Sheriff Wash Thompson and a squad of deputies and Chief of Police George O. Purdy of East St. Louis, and a platoon of policemen, have searched the country between the river and the Bluffs for the negro.

The farmers are armed with shot-guns and revolvers and they are desperate. Over 100 negroes have been arrested, but all have been released as they either proved an alibi for the day, or failed to fit the description and gave good accounts of themselves.

According to several of the farmers living in the neighborhood, it is thought that the double crime was committed by the same negro. A negro answering the above description, and which tallies with that given by the negress, was said to have been seen by several persons, for the last three days, in the neighborhood of the Bruno farm.

INQUEST IS HELD.

Coroner McCracken held an inquest over the body of Miss Bruno yesterday afternoon. A verdict of death, the result of a fractured skull, was returned. The blame for the injury was attached to a party or parties unknown.

There has been much excitement in both East St. Louis and Belleville as a result of the double crime, and Sheriff Thompson has stated that he will swear in as many deputies as are needed to protect the negro, if arrested and placed in his hands.

It is openly stated in East St. Louis that if the farmers get the negro before the authorities, he will be shot.

HAPPENINGS IN EAST SIDE CITIES AND TOWNS NEGRESS IDENTIFIES CROSS AS MAN WHO ASSAULTED HER From Twelve Others She Picks Out the Negro Charged With Stay ing Florence Bruno.
In the Belleville jail yesterday afternoon Annie Green, the negress who was assaulted in a similar manner to the assault on Florence Bruno, the white girl who was found dead at her home near Fireworks Station, near East St. Louis, looked up and down a row of negro prisoners and without hesitation walked up to and put her hand on James Cross, the negro arrested by the East St. Louis police on the charge of committing the double crime.

"That is the man who almost killed me," declared the young negress.

Annie Green and Florence Bruno were assaulted in their homes, near Fireworks Station, on June 23. The assaults were similar and the white girl was found dead. Her head had been fractured and she was otherwise injured.

Annie Green was taken to the Henrietta Hospital, where she lay between life and death for several weeks.

On June 25 Chief Purdy and several of his men, who were working on the case, arrested James Cross. His general description tallied with that given by the negress of the man who assaulted her. When taken before her at the hospital, he was identified by her as the man, but he denied it vehemently. The news of the arrest of the man was kept quiet by Chief Purdy, who feared an attempt might be made to get possession of the negro by the friends of the Bruno family.

Yesterday, as a final test of the Green woman's ability to identify the negro who she alleges assaulted her, she was brought to Belleville. A dozen negro prisoners of the same general appearance as Cross were marshaled in the jailer's office, with Cross placed in the middle of the bunch. Then the young woman was called and was asked if the man who assaulted her was in the party. She walked up to the line, and without the slightest hesitation pointed out Cross.

Two Are Mortally Wounded and Number Injured on Both Sides.
TROUBLE RESULTED FROM
THE KELLAR INJUNCTION
Officers Were Attempting to Serve Papers for Violating the Order of the Court and the Rioting Miners Resisted.
Charleston, Kanawha County, W. Va., February 25.—At Stanniford City, in Raleigh county, at dawn this morning, a terrible battle took place between the joint posses of Deputy United States Marshal Cunningham and Sheriff Cook on one side and rioting miners on the other, as a result of which three miners were killed, two others mortally wounded and a number of others on both sides more or less seriously hurt.

The killed:
Dick Taylor.

Mortally wounded:
John Heiser and Irwin Lawson.

The trouble grew out of the attempt to arrest thirty-four miners for violation of the blanket injunction by Federal Judge Kellar last August.

Cause of the Trouble.

On last Saturday Deputy Marshal D. W. Cunningham went to Atkinsville, a mining town in Raleigh county, to arrest men charged with violating the injunction. He was surrounded by a large party of miners armed with Winchester rifles, who ordered him to leave the place, an order which he quickly obeyed. Sheriff Cook about the same time attempted to make some arrests under process issued by the state court and was treated in a like manner.

Cunningham returned to this city and reported to the marshal and district attorney that he could do nothing without a large force, and then only at imminent risk of precipitating a bloody conflict. He was instructed to return with men sufficient to serve the process given him and to do it at all hazards. Before Cunningham returned to Atkinsville, however, Marshal John K. Thompson and S. C. Burdette, attorney for the United Mine Workers went to the scene, spending most of Sunday and Monday there. They found everything quiet, the rioters having withdrawn from the immediate neighborhood and crossed New River, going into camp 300 strong near the "Big Q" mine on the north side.

Strong Posse Organized.

Thompson and Burdette came home Tuesday morning, and Cunningham and a strong posse went from here to make the arrests. When Atkinsville was reached the federal forces were joined by Sheriff Cook and his posse, the coal companies nearby furnishing several guards, and the sheriff and his deputies found themselves in command of about 100 well-armed and determined men. The rioters had recrossed the river on Tuesday, and were parading up and down before the various coal works, from 150 to 200 men, armed with Winchesters. They intimidated miners at work, drove away guards of the mines and even went so far as to disarm a guard and force him to march at the head of their procession. Emboldened by their success, they attempted to burn a bridge of the Chesapeake and Ohio railroad over Piney Gulch, and threatened the destruction of other property. Last night they went into camp near Stanniford City.

This morning about daybreak the officers and their combined posse, surprised the rioters in their camp and called on them to surrender. The reply was a shot. This was answered by a shot and immediately a furious battle was raging. When it ceased three of the rioters lay dead and many others were found to be wounded, two of them fatally.

Seventy-three Arrests Made.

Seventy-three arrests were made, ten falling to the share of Deputy Cunningham and sixty-three to that of Sheriff Cook. All of the prisoners were taken to Beckley, the county seat of Raleigh, where the ten United States prisoners were given a preliminary hearing by Commissioner Dunn and held for their appearance at court here. They will be brought here on an early morning train.

The federal authorities will try to get the state to give up the sixty-three so that they may be tried in the federal court, but it is doubtful whether it will be done as the State court meets on Monday, and it is thought, they can probably be tried more expeditiously there.

S. S. Burdette, attorney for the mine workers of America, went to Beckley this evening to attend to the case of the miners.

The injunction which the miners were charged with violating was the blanket writ issued by Judge B. F. Kellar at the suit of the Chesapeake and Ohio Coal Agency company last August. The defendants in the case were all the coal companies operating in the New River field, a hundred and fifty of the United Mine Workers of America by name, including President Mitchell and Secretary Wilson and all other persons whosoever aided and abetted them. The injunction covered almost every foot of ground in the coal-mining region of New River. While all of the mines in the Kanawha and New River sections have been at work for some months, the strike has not been officially declared off and its embers have been smoldering in the New River gorge, threatening to break into flame in the spring.

The locality in which today's tragedy occurred is one in which the mines have but recently been opened up and the small towns are filled with the most desperate men that have ever come into the state.

Advices from the scene of the conflict tonight are to the effect that all is quiet now, but fears are entertained that trouble will break out afresh at any moment and the conflict of today is thought to be the forerunner of many more to come in the near future.

OFFICIAL REPORT

Investigation of the Killing of
Negro Miners

FEELING AGAINST MARSHAL

Report Says Evans Went to the Scene at Atkinsville and Found Forty-eight Men Had Been Arrested for Conspiracy.
FEELING AGAINST MARSHAL
Indianapolis, March 8.—The official report of Chris Evans, who was sent to the West Virginia coal fields to investigate the killing of the colored miners at Atkinsville, has been received at the headquarters of the United Mine Workers.

The report says that General St. Clare, who is the attorney for the coal companies, created an agitation to have the men arrested and taken to Charleston, and that immediately afterward arrangements were made with the United States marshal by the mine workers officials to give bond for all who were arrested, but that later, on account of the agitation created by Deputy Marshal Cunningham, the agreement entered into with the marshal was broken and Cunningham was sent to arrest the men.

According to the report there was great feeling against Cunningham, and the men decided not to allow him to arrest them, and he was driven away. Mr. Evans says that he sent a telegram to the men to submit quietly, but that the coal companies, who own all of the telegraph and telephone lines connecting with the town, refused to deliver it, and before he could send a message to the men, Cunningham and his deputies, whom he says were the worst characters he could collect, went to the town a second time and killed the miners in the night time in their beds. Mr. Evans says he went to the scene of the trouble the next morning, and that forty-eight men had been arrested for conspiracy to kill Cunningham and found there in a house occupied by a colored man called "Stonewall" Jackson, the dead bodies of William Dodson, William Clark and Richard Clayton, all colored.

Shots Fired Into House.

The report continues: "On inquiry we found the wife of Jackson with four children, together with eight colored men were in the house, and that about daybreak all that were inside were awakened by shots being fired into the house from the outside. This shooting took place without anything being said to those on the inside and the three colored men I have mentioned were found dead on the floor. Two were in their night clothes and the other one was partly dressed, with one shoe on partly laced, and the other foot bare. We visited another house where Joseph Hizer lay in bed, mortally wounded, having been shot through the window as he was stooping to put his trousers on after getting out of bed. Hizer lived with his sister and she made the statement at the inquest that she pleaded with those shooting not to kill her children and in reply Cunningham said: 'Women and children must take care of themselves.' In no instance could we find where these people had been asked to surrender until after the deputies had commenced shooting all the occupants of the houses named.

"We next went to the house of Lucian Lawson, who was considered mortally wounded. I am led to understand that after the shooting referred to, this man, with others, returned the fire of the posse and this is the only instance where any attempt was made to return the fire on the part of the miners. During the shooting in many instances the men and women pleaded with the men outside to have mercy on them, but their cries were met with derision and curses. Our investigation proves conclusively that no effort had been made to shoot or resist except in the one case mentioned, but that all would have been too glad to have surrendered if they had been allowed the opportunity to do so." Mr. Evans says that the coroner's jury has returned a verdict of felonous killing against Cunningham for the killing of William Dodson.

Charleston, W. Va., March 20.—The report of the federal grand jury, which has been investigating the riots in which five men were killed and others badly injured, was made public tonight after first having been submitted to Attorney General Knox and President Roosevelt, in Washington, by United States Attorney Atkinson. The report is given by permission of Attorney General Knox. It says:

"On February 21, D. W. Cunningham, deputy United States marshal, went to Atkinsville to execute certain writs. He was met by an armed mob and informed that he would not be permitted to execute said writs and his life was threatened. When he protested against such proceedings the alarm bell was rung over the hall of the United Mine Workers, which seems to have been a preconcerted signal, an dhew ETAburnedfilraflhinGv signal, and he was immediately surrounded by an angry mob of armed men and ordered to leave the town in five minutes under penalty of death, if he did not do so and one of the mob beat up his gun which was cocked, with the avowed intention of killing him and was only prevented from doing so by the action of one of the members of the unoin, who had taken no part in the threatened demonstration, in catching the man with the gun by the coat, jerking him back and finally wrestling the gun from him.

"This same band of men or mob organized themselves into a semi-military body and marched across the country to a rendezvous on Big Mountain, near Quinnmont.

"A crowd of men estimated from 200 to 300 assembled and camped on Big Mountain. A portion of them, some 150 nearly all of whom were armed, started from there on the morning of February 24. They appeared to be under strict military discipline and were commanded by men who evidently had had some military discipline or experience. They marched with military precision from Big Mountain direct to Stanford City, where the yarrived about or shortly after nightfall, February 24. 1903.

"Having been informed of this proceeding and having learned that the men for whom they had proceses were members of the mob, Deputy Marshal Cunningham gathered together a number of men as a posse comitatus, some twenty or more, and left for Stanford City on the evening of February 24 and went to Raleigh, where they were joined by Harvey Cook, sheriff of Raleigh county, with a posse comitatus of some sixty or more. By arrangement between Deputy Marshal Cunningham and Sheriff Cook, the county posse was added to the marshal's posse and the deputy marshal's posse was made a part of the constabulary or posse comitatus of Raleigh county.

"We have examined a large number of witnesses who were present and participated in what took place at Atkinsville on Feb. 21, which culminated in the battle at Stanaford City on the morning of Feb. 25, 1903. This evidence before us as to what occurred at Atkinsville was not only from United States Deputy Marshals, but from citizens of Raleigh county and members of the miners' union and was uncontradicted and irrefutable. On that day D. W. Cunningham, Deputy United States Marshal, went to Atkinsville to execute certain writs placed in his hands, issued from your honor's court; he was met by an armed mob and informed that he would not be permitted to execute said writs, and his life was threatened.

Mob of Armed Men.

"When he protested against such proceedings and informed them that he was an officer of the law, trying to perform his duty, the alarm bell was rung and he was immediately surrounded by an angry mob of armed men and ordered to leave the town in five minutes under penalty of death, and one of the mob threw up his gun, which was cocked, with the avowed intention of killing him and was only prevented from doing so by one of the members of the miners' union. THE LILY WHITES IN THE NORTH.

It is out of the ordinary to find an Iowa paper pleading for an "all white" town, but that is the burden of the leading editorial in a recent issue of the Waterloo Courier. Admitting that Waterloo has a considerable colored population of fairly good citizens, the Courier favors discouraging a negro colony in Waterloo and calls attention to the effect of the recent baseball games in which negro players took part, as encouraging negro immigration. "If Waterloo does not want them," continues the Courier, "their coming here should be discouraged. The race question is assuming a threatening character in various parts of the country; the antagonism is certain to increase rather than diminish. The exodus of negroes from the south and even from portions of Illinois, Indiana and Ohio is growing. Let Waterloo keep perfectly white and as long as she can. But this condition can not long be maintained if negro baseball teams are invited here to stand on an equal footing with the white teams. It acts as an advertisement for others to come, and even the least encouragement to a negro settlement in this city should be discounted."

Perhaps the Courier is right and an infusion of negro population into a northern city is detrimental to its best interests. There is something, however, in the proposal to deny the right of residence to any respectable citizen in account of color that jars on a decent sense of right and justice. The denial to an honest black man of the right to live in a free country because many of his race are disreputable and dishonest violates the fundamentals of democratic government. It is wrong in principle and all that is wrong in the abstract can never become righteous in practice. No city desires the depraved or idle among its citizenship and discrimination against the dishonest and dissolute is a duty communities we themselves. The negro, however, a citizen of the United States under the constitution and entitled by the fundamental law to the rights guaranteed to all Americans. His color should be no bar.

There is a difference between turning men away because they are bad and turning them away because they are black. The one is a justifiable precaution for the defense of society; the other a direct appeal to race prejudice and the forerunner of riot. It is but a step from "discouragement" of immigration to forced emigration. The flame of race prejudice, easiest kindled, is the hardest to subdue. There is a dragon's tooth in every sentence that urges discrimination against color or race.

There are but two practical plans of dealing with the race question. The negro must be bond or free. He must remain a citizen or revert to his old condition of servitude. If he is to continue in citizenship he must be accorded the citizen's right to live honorably wherever the flag floats. There is certain to be an increase of negro immigration into the north and the north that pledged its lives for the black man's freedom must take up its burden unflinchingly. It is no question of desire, but of duty. There is no pale in this republic nor likely to be. The "illy white" policy is not an adaptable one and unfitted to northern intellect and sensibility. The north must take its quota of the colored race and do the best it can with it. Exclusion is practically a confession that the declaration of independence is a falsehood and the constitution a fraud.

No threats were made. The negroes were merely told to go—and they went. No distinction was made between good and bad negroes—all were driven out.

We must appeal from our correspondent's statement that it was the city's "conservative citizens" that were responsible for this lawless action, unless conservative is used in the sense of unprogressive. No conservative citizen ever subscribes to an unlawful, unjust and cruel program. And that it what Waterloo's method of getting rid of the negroes is. From this sort of whitecappery directed at negro citizens the step to arbitrary interference with the rights of white citizens is not a long one.

Among a certain class in Alabama the feeling was that it was at the most a venial offense to enslave negroes by the peonage system. This attitude was summed up in remarking that the victim "was only a nigger."
