LYNCHING WAS NARROWLY AVERTED
Sheriff Summers Evaded Lynchers by Fine Work.
CROWD VISITED THE JAIL
The Negro Was Taken to Charlotte Jail for Safe Keeping---Will be Tried at Irc dell Court Next Week.
(Special to News and Observer.)

(Special to News and Observer.)

Salisbury, N. C., August 3.—The town of Statesville came near witnessing a genuine lynching yesterday afternoon.

Will Roseboro, the negro who brutally assaulted and afterwards murdered Mrs. Dolph Beaver, in Cool Springs township, Iredell county, on last Friday morning, was arrested by Sheriff W. A. Summers on Saturday, near Melrose, Polk county, and was brought to Statesville at 10:40 Sunday morning, and lodged in jail. About six hundred people, most of whom were from the Cool Springs neighborhood, had been watching the incoming trains during Saturday and Sunday for the purpose of capturing the negro culprit and lynching him.

Knowing the sentiment which had been aroused by the crime Sheriff Summers anticipated trouble of this kind and left the train at a point west of Statesville and brought his prisoner to the county jail by a back way and thus avoided the crowd. It is reported, however, that a small company of bystanders who chanced to see the officer entering with the prisoner, attempted to take him from the sheriff who promptly drew his pistol and dispersed the crowd. It soon became known in the community that Roseboro had been placed in the jail and the sheriff soon realized that trouble was brewing. With some difficulty he quietly slipped his prisoner from the jail at 2 p. m., Sunday and left at once in a private conveyance for Mooresville, where he caught a train for Charlotte where Roseboro was placed in jail. At about 5 o'clock a crowd of several hundred persons went to the Ireden jail in search of Roseboro. The deputy in charge of the prison admitted a number of the would-be lynchers who searched in vain for the murderer. Sheriff Summers, who has accomplished a fine piece of official work, returned to Statesville by way of Salisbury at 9:30 last night without having taken food or rest since Friday.

The crime is one of the blackest in the history of the State. Your correspondent has just returned from the scene of the trouble, and many leading citizens were found to be in sympathy with the crowd which would have doubtless lynched the negro, and which was prepared to do the work without disguise or the attempt to conceal their identity.

Mrs. Beaver was a most estimable young woman. Her husband had left home early Friday morning for a business trip to Statesville, and upon his return late that night could not find any trace of his wife. Her morning's work was yet unfinished. A searching party was organized and the body soon found in an old well which had not been used for sometime. The head had been beaten into a jelly on the back and had been crushed on the right side. The hands were badly scratched in an evident struggle with the murderer. The physicians testify to evidence of unspeakable cruelty. Roseboro, who stands charged with the crime, lives only a short distance from the Beaver home, and it is believed that he saw Mr. Beaver leave at about daylight on Friday morning and that he at once committed the awful deed. A pistol which was missing from the house was found in his pocket when arrested. He is now in jail at Charlotte, and as court convenes at Statesville next week, it is hoped by the conservative people of Iredell that the law will be allowed to take its course.

READY TO LYNCH TWO NEGROES
Who Were in Asbury Park Jail for Running Over a Girl.
ASBURY PARK, N. J., July 6.—The residents of Eatontown were ready last night to lynch William Riley and Andrew Kelly, the two colored men who on Saturday ran over Jennie Covert with their wagon. The young girl is very popular in Eatontown. The negroes left her bleeding and senseless on the road. She was picked up by an automobile party and carried at breakneck speed to the Long Branch Hospital, where she still lies unconscious. It is thought that she will die.

The negroes were hunted down and arrested yesterday in West Asbury Park, where they were lodged in the township jail. When the Eatontown friends of Miss Covert heard of the capture they went around looking for wagons and vehicles of every description to carry the indignant citizens to Asbury Park to storm the jail.

Chief Gravatt of the township police received word that a storm was brewing. He hurriedly arraigned the prisoners before Justice Dodd, who held them without bail to await the result of Miss Covert's injuries. Then, securely handcuffed, they were taken out at midnight and driven to Freehold in a closed carriage. It is said that the Eatontown people were much disappointed and turned back with regret. The accident occurred on the Eatontown road. A second auto filled with furious men went after the colored men, but took the wrong road.

william-riley-asbury-park-1903-07-05.A6:
The Lynching Craze.
Friday afternoon an Evansville negro killed a policeman who was trying to arrest him. When a white man kills a policeman the law is allowed to take its course. There is no public frenzy. Negroes belong to the widening jurisdiction of Judge Lynch. The long series of hangings and burnings of negroes has put the "suggestion" of lynching into the mind of the crowd. So a mob sprang up in Evansville. It had no thought of waiting for the courts. It had no notion of leaving to their orderly inquest and process the determination of the guilt and punishment of this negro. It did not know or care whether he had resisted arrest lawfully or unlawfully. His original and unpardonable sin was his color. He was a negro. He must be put out of the way.

The mob and the hysteria of the mob grew fiercer from Friday to Monday. By Sunday night riot ruled. Monday night the county jail was stormed. The militia company called to its defence by a Sheriff equal to his duty was fired upon. It answered, and seven lawbreakers and would-be murderers were killed and four wounded dangerously.

Governor Durbin showed none of the weakness of so many public officers who are afraid to injure their political prospects by interfering with a few thousand of their fellow citizens, insane with negrophobia. He sent a battery company and some Gatling guns to the jail, and threatened to come at once and declare martial law if order was not restored. Evansville needed martial law Monday night. The mob broke into the firearms stores. Crazy speeches were made. For thousands of men the rule of law had ended temporarily.

A good deal is said by the apologists of lynching about negroes as "the wild beasts." Is there any wilder beast than that many-headed beast the mob? The appetite for hanging, torturing and burning negroes grows with what it feeds on. Each lynching begets new ones, for more trivial causes.

Evansville goes mad from the contagion of the lynching madness elsewhere. Are the Americans losing their instinct of self-control and self-government? Are they indeed "a violent people," as Mr. BAYARD once called them to their great indignation?

Brave Governors and Sheriffs and Gatling guns can do something to keep down these outbreaks of savagery. But what disgrace is put upon Americans almost every day! The disorders are not sporadic. The mob is becoming almost the regular executioner of negroes. If this is a Government of law, the mob must be cowed or shot down.

These acts of tumultuary violence for the moment are directed against the negro. But they are dangerous symptoms. Everywhere the reliance upon law is weakening. Almost everywhere the germs of mob madness may be detected. A motorman runs over a child. "Lynch him!" yells the crowd instinctively. The mob spirit, so ferocious in Evansville, exists in quiet New Jersey towns. Citizens of Netcong tried to lynch some Italians. In Asbury Park, Monday morning, a mob threatened three negroes who had ridden down a young woman; a mob of respectable farmers. If the girl dies, they say, they will lynch the negroes. It is a fact that the lynching craze is everywhere. It must stop.

NEGRO LYNCHED FOR MURDER.
Posse Hired a River Steamer to Catch Him Sheriff Saw Him Hanged.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 16.—William Washington, the negro who killed a white man named Stanley Woods, near Talbert, on last Monday, was lynched last night, a short distance beyond the Louisiana-Mississippi line in Mississippi. The killing of Woods occurred immediately on the State line, Washington fled to Louisiana and crossed the Mississippi into Pointe Coupee Parish. A mob of seventy-five men on horseback and with bloodhounds started in pursuit.

The steamer Betsey Ann was hired and Washington traced to Red River Landing, La., where he was captured. He was then taken into Mississippi, a short distance across the State line, and hanged to a tree. He confessed to killing Woods, but said he was drunk at the time. The Sheriff of West Feliciana was present at the lynching, but was unable to prevent it.
